question.prompt:
Three distinct lines intersect at the same point \(O\). Counting each angle smaller than a straight angle formed by any two noncollinear rays as one angle, how many pairs of vertical angles are there in the figure?

[Figure 1](figures/cnm_063_q5_question_en.svg)

solutions.explanation: The three lines give \(6\) distinct rays. To count each pair of rays once, put the rays in any order and pair each ray only with rays later in that order. This gives \(5+4+3+2+1=15\) pairs. Exactly three pairs consist of opposite rays, one pair on each line, so they form excluded straight angles. Thus the total number of angles smaller than a straight angle is \(15-3=12\). Each angle has exactly one vertical angle, so there are \(12\div2=6\) pairs.
solutions.title: Count angles, then pair them

solutions.explanation: Group the vertical-angle pairs by the two lines containing their sides. Call the three lines \(l_1,l_2,l_3\). Their possible pairs are \((l_1,l_2)\), \((l_1,l_3)\), and \((l_2,l_3)\). Each line pair forms four angles smaller than a straight angle, which pair off into two pairs of vertical angles. Every vertical-angle pair uses exactly one of these line pairs, so all are counted once. Therefore there are \(3\times2=6\) pairs.
solutions.title: Group by pairs of lines
